transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2027-04-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
End: 15:48 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Reed (Redwood AE), Priya Menon (Redwood SE), Sam Torres (Redwood Solutions), Maya Patel (CTO, Cerulean), Diego Alvarez (Head of Infra), Rita Singh (Security), Tom Weber (ML Eng)
Links referenced: https://redwood.ai/internal/papers/private-link-vs-peering (shared), Cerulean-genomics-network.xlsx (customer)

Summary:
- Kickoff scoping for a Private deployment pilot focused on strict data residency and egress controls.
- Primary evaluation: VPC peering vs PrivateLink, regional constraints (EU-only), and an egress-bounded landing zone for ML inference benchmarks.
- Success criteria: <48ms p95 for 512-token gen on prod-ish model variant, no cross-region egress, audit logs for every request, and max monthly infra delta under the committed spend.

Topics:
- Workload sizing and expected TPS
- Benchmarks and measurement plan
- Network connectivity options (peering vs PrivateLink)
- Region locking and egress firewalling
- Security and compliance (KMS, audit logs, SOC2)
- Timeline and next steps

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Alex Reed: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we have about 45 minutes, so we'll run through the desired pilot outcomes and then dive into the network options and the bench plan. Maya, want to give a quick context on Cerulean's constraints?
[00:18] Maya Patel: Yeah thanks Alex. So quick overview: we're processing patient-derived sequencing meta not raw reads but associated reports. Data can't leave EU data centers. We need strict egress control, plus auditability for every inference. Timeline: hope to have a pilot in two to three weeks to validate perf and residency.
[00:40] Priya Menon: Got it. And when you say pilot, is this for latency-sensitive production or more for batch scoring?
[00:46] Tom Weber: It's primarily real-time-ish. We have a UI that needs sub-100ms p50, but long-term p95 is more meaningful. For benching, we want to simulate peak of 70 TPS sustained for 10 minutes and short bursts to 200 TPS.
[01:05] Diego Alvarez: Right, and infra wise we run in eu-central-1 and eu-west-1. Ideally we'd keep everything in eu-central-1, but we might replicate to eu-west-1 for DR as long as replication is closed circuit and we can prove residency.
[01:20] Rita Singh: Security note — all keys must be customer-controlled KMS, and we need request-level audit logs forwarded to our SIEM. Also we'll want SAML SSO for the console and RBAC.
[01:32] Alex Reed: Good, that aligns with Redwood Private capabilities. Quick thing to flag — we can support customer-managed KMS and we can route logs to your syslog or S3 in the same region. We'll talk about the exact flow in the diagram.
[01:45] Sam Torres: For the pilot success criteria can we capture them now? It helps avoid ambiguity. I'll read out a rough list and you can tweak: 1) residency: no egress from eu region, 2) perf: p95 under 48ms for the 512 token path, 3) audit: request logs available with 24h retention in your log bucket, 4) cost: pilot costs within agreed cap.
[02:07] Maya Patel: Sounds good yes, but p95 48ms seems aggressive. That's for the quantized model? Which model are you sizing for?
[02:16] Priya Menon: We'll run the pilot on two variants: a high-quality LLM-v1 quantized and a smaller latency-optimized variant. The 48ms p95 is our target for the latency variant under a 1 GPU config with our batching policy; the higher-quality model will obviously be slower. We'll include both in the bench.
[02:34] Tom Weber: Okay good. For benchmarking we need the exact prompt templates and a replay dataset of 10k requests representing mix. We'll provide that.
[02:41] Alex Reed: Perfect, please send the dataset anonymized.

Connectivity deep-dive
[03:00] Priya Menon: Let's talk connectivity options — short version: we can do VPC peering or AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints). Peering is simpler from a routing perspective, but PrivateLink can be more controlled from an egress standpoint because traffic never traverses public internet or shared routing zones. Peering allows you to use your native security groups and route tables. PrivateLink gives more strict logical boundary.
[03:22] Diego Alvarez: Our security team prefers PrivateLink because of the more explicit control over ingress, but we're worried about cross-AZ costs and potential limits in endpoint IPs. Also peering would let us use our internal NATs so egress rules are already in place.
[03:38] Rita Singh: Another consideration: our DLP and packet inspection sits in the middle of our NAT egress path. If we use PrivateLink we need to ensure the traffic can be mirrored or logs forwarded to that DLP box — can Redwood support VPC Flow/ENI mirroring?
[03:52] Priya Menon: We can't mirror inside the Redwood-managed subnets, but we can publish detailed request logs and connection metadata to your S3/CloudWatch; you could set up packet capture on your side for any egress that originates from your VPC. For PrivateLink the client keeps the control plane in your VPC for the interface endpoint and connections terminate inside our infra. There is occasionally weirdness with DNS resolution — we'll include the recommended private hosted zone patterns.
[04:15] Alex Reed: Also note our Private product uses a private control plane when in VPC mode; with peering we wire your VPC routes to the worker subnets and you get predictable latency and you maintain egress controls. With PrivateLink we create interface endpoints in your account which you control. There's a slight operational difference around who needs to rotate certs for mTLS and how we do health checks.
[04:35] Maya Patel: Ok so operationally, who touches the certificates?
[04:39] Priya Menon: With peering Redwood handles the right-side certs in our infra; with PrivateLink we can offer customer-provided certs for the endpoint (mutual TLS) so you can centralize rotation with your KMS.
[04:50] Diego Alvarez: Nice. One more: egress policing. We need to ensure no DNS fallbacks to public IPs — if a dependency tries to call an external endpoint we want that to fail. Are you able to support explicit deny lists or egress blackhole at your side?
[05:04] Sam Torres: Yes we can implement egress policy — we can configure the pilot so that only endpoints in eu-central-1 are reachable, and we can do a test harness that tries to reach 8.8.8.8 or other public endpoints to certify. We'll codify that in the test plan.

Bench plan & metrics
[05:25] Priya Menon: For benchmarks we'll run three phases: Baseline cold start (no KV), Steady-state throughput with batching and KV warm, and Failover/resilience checks. Metrics we'll capture: p50/p95/p99 latency, CPU/GPU util, batch sizes, token throughput, and network egress bytes. We'll also surface per-request audit ID.
[05:45] Tom Weber: We care about per-request cost too — token cost isn't the only thing, it's GPU time. Can you annotate token-level timing?
[05:51] Priya Menon: We'll provide token breakdowns and kernel-level timings where possible; some of that is sample-level privacy sensitive but can be redacted.

Region locking and residency proofs
[06:10] Alex Reed: On region locking, Redwood Private can enforce region affinity and deny cross-region routing. For audit we can create a signed manifest of where workloads ran per window. That should help your compliance team prove residency.
[06:24] Rita Singh: Signed manifest is good; can the manifest be cryptographically signed with our KMS?
[06:28] Alex Reed: Yes, we can produce the manifest and then sign it with a customer-controlled key via an integration to your KMS in the pilot. We'll note that as a deliverable.

Operational concerns & roles
[06:45] Diego Alvarez: Day-to-day, who triages incidents? If latency goes high in the pilot, how do we alert and who takes action?
[06:50] Sam Torres: For pilot we'll set up an on-call rotation where Redwood support + your on-call are both paged. We'll also configure traces into your tracing backend via OTLP if you'd like.
[07:02] Maya Patel: We will need SSO into the console for our engineers and RBAC so only a few can trigger model rollouts.
[07:10] Alex Reed: SAML SSO and RBAC are supported; we'll share our setup guide.

Risks and mitigations
[07:20] Priya Menon: A few risks we typically see: DNS fallbacks causing egress, misconfigured security groups causing packet loss, and under-sized batch config creating suboptimal GPU utilization. Mitigations: DNS hardening checks, test harness for egress probes, and tuning batch windows during the steady-state bench.
[07:38] Tom Weber: About batch tuning — we don't want undue latency variability. What's Redwood's recommended max batch latency for real-time UI?
[07:45] Priya Menon: We recommend a micro-batching policy with 8–12ms max batch delay for UI paths; that usually gives good p95 without hurting latency. We'll tune that in the second phase.

Detailed timeline proposal
[08:00] Alex Reed: Proposed timeline if we start this week:
- Day 1–2: Exchange network details, landing zone diagram finalized (customer provides CIDRs)
- Day 3–5: Setup PrivateLink or peering in a dev pilot VPC, install KMS integration and logging
- Day 6–8: Baseline benches and steady-state runs
- Day 9–12: Failover tests, manifest signing, and final report
Maya, does that fit your two-to-three week ask?
[08:35] Maya Patel: Yes that's fine, though our security review may add a few days. If we can run the baseline in the next Monday window it'd help.

Questions from Cerulean
[08:50] Rita Singh: A few quick Qs — 1) can we bring our HSM / external KMS? 2) Will Redwood's control plane ever leave eu-central-1? 3) Are there any required egress IP ranges we need to allow?
[09:05] Priya Menon: 1) Yes, HSM/KMS bring-your-own supported for secret rotation. 2) For private deployments the control plane can be constrained to your region; for hosted we do multi-region control plane but that's not applicable here. We'll confirm exact control plane placement in the doc. 3) If using peering, no additional egress IPs — it's direct routing; if PrivateLink we will share a small set of endpoint IPs but those remain in your account as ENIs. We'll include exact CIDR/IPs in the networking doc.

Noise and small transcription artifacts (speaker overlap)
[09:33] Speaker 1: uh mm yeah
[09:36] Speaker 2: sorry go ahead

Recap & explicit next steps
[09:40] Sam Torres: Quick recap: Alex will share the landing zone diagram and PrivateLink vs peering doc; Priya will publish the benchmark plan; Diego will share CIDRs; Rita will send compliance checklist. We'll tentatively schedule the bench for 2027-04-20.
[09:56] Maya Patel: Confirming 4/20 works for us as a target for the baseline run; we'll try to get you the network info by 4/15.
[10:04] Alex Reed: Great. I'll also include a short runbook for verifying egress posture (simple curl tests and DNS probes) and the manifest signing flow. Expect email with attachments tomorrow.
[10:14] Tom Weber: One last ask — include the expected token-level timings and an example trace for a 512-token sample.
[10:20] Priya Menon: Will do.

End of meeting
[10:30] Alex Reed: Thanks everyone, we will follow up with the docs and set the bench window.
[10:34] Maya Patel: Thanks all.

Notes on transcription quality: some brand names and acronyms may be slightly off (e.g., 'Redwood Private' was sometimes transcribed as 'Woodland Private'), filler words and overlaps preserved.
